question: Can an LLM agent reduce the data-construction, exploration, and credit-assignment costs of reinforcement learning in previously unspecified tool environments by generating its own tasks, reusing distilled trajectory experience, and assigning LLM-judged rewards to individual action steps?

key_findings.claim: The paper's central contribution is an end-to-end agent-training stack that combines self-questioning, self-navigating, and self-attributing rather than a single new reinforcement-learning estimator.
key_findings.evidence: Self-questioning explores an environment profile and turns feasible exploration paths into preference-conditioned tasks and reference solutions; self-navigating mixes vanilla and retrieved-experience rollouts, strips experience text before optimization, and selectively relaxes the positive-advantage clipping bound; self-attributing asks a separate LLM to label every action GOOD or BAD, normalizes the labels and terminal outcome separately, and broadcasts cumulative step rewards to response tokens. The infrastructure then connects task, rollout, experience, environment, and trainer services.

key_findings.claim: Under the paper's own two-benchmark protocol, the complete 7B and 14B systems substantially outperform their corresponding zero-shot Qwen2.5 backbones.
key_findings.evidence: Table 1 reports macro-average avg@8/best@8 of 45.2/60.1 for AgentEvolver-7B versus 15.8/24.0 for zero-shot Qwen2.5-7B, and 57.6/73.1 for AgentEvolver-14B versus 29.8/42.8 for zero-shot Qwen2.5-14B. On AppWorld, complete-system avg@8 is 32.4 for 7B and 48.7 for 14B; on BFCL v3 it is 57.9 and 66.5. These are percentage-point differences inside this study, not relative-percent gains and not comparisons with contemporary agent-RL systems.

key_findings.claim: Synthetic self-questioning tasks can approach or exceed original-task training in some cells, but the result is benchmark- and model-dependent; the strongest result comes from hybrid data rather than synthetic data alone.
key_findings.evidence: Table 2 gives synthetic-versus-original macro avg@8 of 36.1 versus 37.5 for 7B and 52.3 versus 57.4 for 14B. Synthetic data is stronger on AppWorld for 7B (23.2 versus 16.1) and nearly matches the 14B original result (44.3 versus 46.1), but is weaker on BFCL for both sizes (49.0 versus 58.8; 60.3 versus 68.6). Hybrid data is best overall at 43.6/56.0 for 7B and 60.7/74.6 for 14B. Thus the author's claim that synthetic performance is close to original data is fair only in aggregate and hides opposite per-benchmark effects.

anchors.section: Table 2 and 7.3.1 effectiveness of synthetic data

key_findings.claim: The cross-domain transfer evidence is asymmetric and does not establish broad capability generalization.
key_findings.evidence: For Qwen2.5-14B, training on AppWorld synthetic tasks yields BFCL avg@8 56.0 versus 60.3 for BFCL-trained data, the cited 4.3-point drop. The reverse transfer is much weaker: BFCL training yields AppWorld 22.9 versus 44.3 under AppWorld training. For 7B, BFCL-to-AppWorld transfer is 1.2, below the 1.8 zero-shot score, while AppWorld-to-BFCL reaches 36.1 versus 29.8 zero-shot. These cells support directional transfer from AppWorld to BFCL, not a symmetric general capability claim.

key_findings.claim: Reference-conditioned LLM judging improves the reported AppWorld score over weaker judge configurations, but the experiment does not validate judge correctness directly.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 12b reports 22.5 for a naive judge without the stated principles or reference, 33.1 after adding the principles but no reference, and 44.3 for the full reference-based judge. No human agreement, false-positive/false-negative analysis, calibration, confidence interval, or adversarial judge test is reported, so downstream policy performance is the only validation signal.

key_findings.claim: Experience-mixed rollout plus selective boosting improves the reported development-set result, and removing selective boosting erases the gain.
key_findings.evidence: On the Qwen2.5-14B development evaluation in Table 4, Navigating reaches macro avg@4/best@4 65.0/79.9 versus 57.2/71.4 for the RL baseline. Navigating without selective boosting scores 56.7/68.5, slightly below the baseline. Experience injection without RL reaches 30.9/51.8 versus 25.2/44.0 zero-shot. The authors also report that increasing the experience fraction improves inference but excessive fractions harm later training; eta=0.5 is selected.

key_findings.claim: The complete dual-channel attribution reward outperforms outcome-only and attribution-only ablations on both reported backbones.
key_findings.evidence: Table 5 reports macro avg@8/best@8 of 47.6/61.2 for Attributing-7B, 41.3/53.6 without attribution reward, and 35.7/51.4 without outcome reward. For 14B the corresponding values are 62.0/75.7, 57.4/71.7, and 53.0/66.9. This supports complementarity within the paper's synthetic-data training setup, although the ablations inherit the same judge, data, and reporting confounds.

anchors.section: 5.3-5.4 composite reward and token mapping, Equations 20-21

key_findings.claim: The paper's sample-efficiency result shows earlier attainment of the baseline's own target, not equal final quality at a fixed sample or compute budget.
key_findings.evidence: Table 6 defines Steps@.9 as steps needed to reach 90% of the baseline's best performance. Attributing needs 40 versus 90 steps on AppWorld and 20 versus 60 on BFCL v3, while the prose reports AUC 46.26 versus 41.03 and 61.02 versus 55.78. Because the threshold is tied to the weaker baseline, this does not show how many samples each method needs to reach the same higher endpoint, and the paper does not translate normalized training steps into trajectories, tokens, judge calls, wall-clock time, or dollars.

key_findings.claim: The context-manager comparison supports adaptive memory handling, but it is a separate Qwen3-14B experiment and not evidence that the three AgentEvolver learning mechanisms caused the gain.
key_findings.evidence: Table 7 uses Qwen3-14B on AppWorld, whereas the main RL tables use Qwen2.5-7B/14B. Self-Context-Managing is best at TGC@8 (.720) and SGC@8 (.607), but Reasoning-Augmented is best at TGC@4 (.661 versus .613) and ties SGC@4 (.500). The table has no training-module factorial and no compute comparison, so it evaluates templates, not the unified self-evolution loop.

key_findings.claim: The attribution method is internally inconsistent about label values and the population used for normalization.
key_findings.evidence: Section 5.2 assigns GOOD=+1 and BAD=-1 and specifies trajectory-level standardization: average labels within each trajectory, then compute statistics over trajectory averages. Section 7.1.3 says BAD is 0 or -1 and that step-level normalization is applied within the group. These choices produce different rewards and advantages; the paper does not state which implementation generated the tables. Degenerate groups are said to be neutralized, but the exact rule is also absent.

key_findings.claim: The reward equations and hyperparameter discussion contain unresolved notation and cross-reference defects.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 20 fixes the terminal-outcome coefficient implicitly at one and weights attribution by alpha; Section 7.1.3 newly calls the outcome weight beta=1 without beta appearing in Equation 20. Section 7.5.3 refers to a composite reward in Equation 23 even though the PDF has no Equation 23 and Equation 20 is the relevant definition. Equation 17 separately uses beta for the KL penalty, overloading the symbol. These defects prevent an exact reconstruction of the stated objective from the manuscript alone.

key_findings.claim: The main ablation design does not identify synergy among all three mechanisms.
key_findings.evidence: Table 1 compares zero-shot, Questioning, Questioning&Navigating, Questioning&Attributing, and the full system. It omits Navigating-only, Attributing-only, Navigating&Attributing without Questioning, and matched independent replications. The full row being highest is compatible with additive effects or correlated changes in data and rewards; it is not a statistical interaction test. Separate tables also switch between test-normal and dev sets and between @8 and @4, limiting cross-table subtraction.

key_findings.claim: The evidence does not establish the advertised cost-effectiveness or autonomy of the learning loop.
key_findings.evidence: Training uses eight A100-80GB GPUs, Qwen-Plus for exploration and task synthesis, Qwen3-235B-A22B as the task judge, and Qwen-Max for step attribution. The paper does not report tokens, task-generation calls, judge calls, rollouts per final score, wall-clock, energy, API price, human environment-profile effort, or total synthetic-data curation cost. Its Next Steps section explicitly says unifying the stages into one model remains future work.

key_findings.claim: The formal proxy-objective section states a design goal, not a theorem that self-generated tasks improve the unknown target distribution.
key_findings.evidence: Equations 4-7 define task and reward mappings and then say they should be formulated so maximizing J_train improves J_target. No identifiability condition, divergence bound between p_train and p_target, convergence result, or safeguard against exploration blind spots is provided. Reference solutions are extracted from paths the exploration model already found, so unseen capabilities and systematic judge errors can remain outside the training distribution.

key_findings.claim: The paper's novelty and baseline framing are too broad because earlier direct systems already cover self-evolving curricula, multi-turn agent RL, experience replay, and step-level credit assignment.
key_findings.evidence: The manuscript has no dedicated related-work comparison and evaluates only same-backbone zero-shot and vanilla-GRPO rows. It cites GiGPO and Tool-R1 but does not benchmark against them, and omits direct earlier systems including WebRL, RAGEN, Agent Lightning, and AgentRR. The defensible novelty is the particular integration and its selective experience-stripping/boosting plus LLM-attribution implementation, not the first self-evolving agent, first task-generating agent RL system, first experience-reusing agent, or first fine-grained agent credit method.

method.core_idea: Move initiative in agent reinforcement learning from a fixed human dataset and undifferentiated terminal reward to an LLM-guided loop that discovers feasible tasks, retrieves reusable natural-language experience, and retrospectively labels the contribution of each action.
method.mechanism: Self-questioning uses an environment profile, high-temperature breadth-then-depth exploration, preference-conditioned task synthesis, reference-solution extraction, lexical/semantic deduplication, and replay-based feasibility filtering. Self-navigating builds a validated vector-store experience pool, retrieves and rewrites top-k experiences, mixes guided and unguided rollouts, strips experience text before gradient computation, and expands the positive-advantage PPO/GRPO clipping ceiling for guided samples. Self-attributing prompts a judge over the whole trajectory, converts GOOD/BAD step labels into a normalized process channel, separately normalizes the terminal outcome, sums future composite rewards into step advantages, and broadcasts them to tokens. A Ray-backed service stack supplies environment actors, rollout/context managers, experience management, and veRL-based optimization.
assumptions: An environment profile accurately exposes the entities, attributes, and operations users care about.
High-temperature LLM exploration reaches states representative of an unknown target task distribution rather than only states already easy for the explorer.
A task synthesized after a successful path and replayed once is semantically valid, non-leaky, and representative of future user goals.
The exploration trajectory can serve as a trustworthy reference solution even when alternate valid paths exist.
Qwen-family proprietary judges reliably score long tool trajectories and attribute causal contribution to individual actions from observational traces.
Natural-language experiences retrieved by embedding similarity apply to the current state and do not suppress novel exploration.
Removing experience tokens creates an off-policy mismatch that can be safely handled by selectively increasing the clipping ceiling for positive-advantage samples.
Binary process labels contain enough information to improve credit assignment and do not merely reproduce the terminal judge's preferences.
The stated normalization population and BAD-label encoding match the implementation despite contradictory descriptions.
AppWorld and BFCL v3 capture the long-horizon agent behaviors needed to support broader self-evolution claims.
Eight rollouts and best@k reporting provide a meaningful capability measure despite deployment-time sampling cost.
Changes across sequential module rows are attributable to the named module despite incomplete factorial controls and unreported uncertainty.
External judge and exploration model costs can be ignored when describing the resulting policy-training process as cost-effective.
Context compression or deletion preserves every dependency needed for later actions.
Synthetic and target data can be advantage-weighted together without introducing reward-scale or distribution bias.

techniques.role: Constrains open-ended exploration to named entities, attributes, and conceptual operations.
Uses early breadth and later myopic depth with a high-temperature LLM to collect diverse environment trajectories.
Transforms exploration traces into tasks whose difficulty and style follow user rubrics.
Condenses a discovered path into a reference solution for reward judging and feasibility replay.
Combines lexical/semantic duplicate checks and environment replay to reject redundant or infeasible tasks.
Mixes synthetic proxy tasks with available target-distribution tasks and downweights synthetic advantages.
Scores long trajectories after relevance/repetition checks by comparing critical steps with a discovered reference.
Extracts, validates, embeds, retrieves, reranks, and rewrites reusable advice from successful and failed trials.
Interleaves retrieved-experience and vanilla trajectories to tune the exploration-exploitation balance.
Removes retrieved advice from optimization prompts so the policy must internalize rather than copy it.
Raises the PPO/GRPO importance-ratio ceiling only for positive-advantage experience-guided samples.
Labels each action GOOD or BAD in one whole-trajectory judge call.
Normalizes process attribution and terminal outcome separately before fusing them.
Maps cumulative future step rewards to every response token belonging to the action.
Maintains editable working context while immutable timeline snapshots preserve loss-aligned rollout history.
Lets the policy keep, delete, or externally compress old messages when the context budget is reached.

evaluations.setting: AppWorld test-normal and BFCL v3 multi-turn; Qwen2.5-7B/14B policies, maximum 30 steps, eight independent rollouts per instance (pp. 18-20)
evaluations.metric: Task Goal Completion avg@8 and best@8 in percent, plus the unweighted mean across benchmarks.
evaluations.result: Complete AgentEvolver: 7B AppWorld 32.4/51.2, BFCL 57.9/69.0, macro 45.2/60.1; 14B AppWorld 48.7/69.4, BFCL 66.5/76.7, macro 57.6/73.1. Zero-shot backbones: 7B macro 15.8/24.0; 14B macro 29.8/42.8.
evaluations.baseline: Same-backbone zero-shot Qwen2.5 and sequential Questioning, Questioning&Navigating, and Questioning&Attributing ablations; no external agent-RL competitor.

evaluations.setting: Synthetic-task study on AppWorld and BFCL with Qwen2.5-7B/14B (pp. 20-21)
evaluations.metric: avg@8/best@8 TGC by synthetic, original target, and hybrid training data.
evaluations.result: 7B macro: original 37.5/49.8, synthetic 36.1/50.5, hybrid 43.6/56.0. 14B macro: original 57.4/68.0, synthetic 52.3/68.8, hybrid 60.7/74.6.
evaluations.baseline: Zero-shot and training on original target-distribution tasks.

evaluations.setting: AppWorld synthetic-data volume and LLM-judge component analyses (pp. 20-22)
evaluations.metric: Reported performance curve for 100/200/500 tasks and best@8-like judge-configuration score.
evaluations.result: Data-volume curve rises 40.3 to 42.7 to 44.3 as volume grows 100 to 200 to 500. Judge scores are 22.5 naive, 33.1 with principles but no reference, and 44.3 with principles plus reference. No dispersion or direct label-quality statistic is supplied.
evaluations.baseline: Lower synthetic-data volumes and weaker LLM-judge prompts.

evaluations.setting: Cross-domain training on AppWorld versus BFCL synthetic tasks, evaluated on both benchmarks (p. 21)
evaluations.result: 14B AppWorld-trained to BFCL: 56.0/68.9 versus BFCL-trained 60.3/72.1; BFCL-trained to AppWorld: 22.9/40.8 versus AppWorld-trained 44.3/65.5. The 7B BFCL-trained AppWorld avg@8 is 1.2, below 1.8 zero-shot.

evaluations.setting: Qwen2.5-14B development-set self-navigating ablation on AppWorld and BFCL; four rollouts (pp. 22-23)
evaluations.metric: avg@4/best@4 TGC and learning curves under experience fractions and clipping ceilings.
evaluations.result: Macro 65.0/79.9 for Navigating versus 57.2/71.4 RL baseline and 56.7/68.5 without selective boosting. The chosen eta=.5 balances later training, and epsilon-hat-high=.6 is selected over .4/.8/1.0 from qualitative curves.
evaluations.baseline: Zero-shot without/with retrieved experience, vanilla RL, and Navigating without selective boosting.

evaluations.setting: Self-attributing ablation on synthetic AppWorld development data and BFCL v3 using Qwen2.5-7B/14B (p. 24)
evaluations.result: 7B complete 47.6/61.2, outcome-only 41.3/53.6, attribution-only 35.7/51.4. 14B complete 62.0/75.7, outcome-only 57.4/71.7, attribution-only 53.0/66.9.
evaluations.baseline: Untrained backbone, outcome-only reward, and attribution-only reward.

evaluations.setting: Qwen2.5-14B equal normalized training-budget curves on AppWorld and BFCL v3 (p. 25)
evaluations.metric: Steps@.9 of the baseline's best score and area under the learning curve.
evaluations.result: Attributing versus baseline Steps@.9: 40 versus 90 on AppWorld and 20 versus 60 on BFCL. Reported AUC: 46.26 versus 41.03 and 61.02 versus 55.78. Exact rollout, token, and judge-call counts are absent.
evaluations.baseline: Outcome-only GRPO under the same normalized plotted budget.

evaluations.setting: Qwen3-14B AppWorld comparison of four context-managing templates (p. 26)
evaluations.result: Basic .435/.506 and .268/.375; Reasoning-Augmented .661/.690 and .500/.571; Sliding-Window .560/.601 and .393/.411; Self-Context-Managing .613/.720 and .500/.607.
evaluations.baseline: Basic causal, reasoning-augmented, sliding-window, and self-context-managing templates.

limitations: Author-stated: validation is limited to AppWorld and BFCL; higher-complexity enterprise, safety-critical, and interleaved objectives are future work (p. 27).
Author-stated: scaling to larger policy models and measuring compute-data trade-offs remains future work (p. 27).
Author-stated: unifying task generation, navigation, attribution, and inference within one model is future work; the present system depends on several external models (p. 27).

Author-stated through sensitivity results: excessive experience-guided rollout fractions and overly large selective-clipping bounds improve early performance but harm later optimization through restricted exploration or overfitting (p. 23).
Author-stated through alpha analysis: a large attribution weight can overfit the LLM judge's heuristic labels and reduce final performance (pp. 25-26).
Reviewer-identified: no seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, per-instance uncertainty, or complete run-selection protocol accompany the main tables.

Reviewer-identified: the method and implementation conflict on BAD-label values and attribution-normalization population, and the objective contains beta overloading plus a nonexistent Equation 23 reference.
Reviewer-identified: incomplete factorial ablations do not identify interaction or synergy among Questioning, Navigating, and Attributing.
Reviewer-identified: same-backbone zero-shot/GRPO baselines do not establish superiority to current direct agent-RL competitors.
Reviewer-identified: cost-effectiveness is not measured despite large proprietary judge/explorer models and eight A100-80GB GPUs.
Reviewer-identified: best@8 combines policy quality with eight-sample inference compute and should not be read as single-run reliability.
Reviewer-identified: task profiles and user preferences are manually supplied, so data construction is reduced but not eliminated or costed.
Reviewer-identified: replay validates executability of one reference path, not semantic correctness, completeness, or absence of alternate valid solutions.
Reviewer-identified: the two benchmarks and Qwen-family policies/judges provide limited architecture, domain, and evaluator independence.
Reviewer-identified: dev, test-normal, @4, and @8 protocols vary across tables, preventing clean numerical composition of module gains.
failure_modes: Environment profiles omit important operations, causing curiosity exploration and the synthetic curriculum to exclude target capabilities permanently.
The explorer finds a feasible but brittle path; the extracted reference then penalizes valid alternate trajectories or teaches the explorer's own blind spots.
The reference-based judge is reward-hacked by verbose step overlap, superficial relevance, or trajectories tailored to the judge rather than the environment tests.
Embedding retrieval selects a superficially similar but inapplicable experience, and experience-guided rollouts concentrate around a wrong strategy.
High experience fraction suppresses exploration and creates the late-training degradation observed in the eta analysis.
Experience stripping makes rollout and training conditionals diverge; relaxed positive clipping amplifies biased or misestimated advantages.
A GOOD/BAD attribution judge mistakes correlation for contribution, labels necessary exploratory detours BAD, or credits redundant steps on successful trajectories.
Near-zero reward variance neutralizes a channel, leaving sparse tasks with no useful gradient.
Long trajectories exceed the attribution judge's context or attention capacity, producing inconsistent early-step labels.
Synthetic tasks drift from real user goals, so J_train improves while J_target stagnates or declines.
A hybrid-data reward-scale mismatch causes synthetic or target tasks to dominate despite the fixed .5 synthetic-advantage decay.
Self-context management deletes or compresses a fact needed much later, yielding irreversible tool actions from incomplete state.
Repeated best-of-eight sampling hides low per-rollout reliability and multiplies deployment cost.
The same model-family biases recur in task generation, judging, attribution, and policy, making apparent agreement circular.
An unsafe or side-effectful task passes replay feasibility because executability is checked without an explicit safety or user-value criterion.
reusable_insights: When external advice is used only to obtain better trajectories, remove it from optimization inputs and explicitly audit the resulting off-policy shift.
Mix guided and unguided rollouts; retrieval can raise immediate success while lowering the diversity required for later policy improvement.
Normalize process and terminal reward channels separately before fusion, but specify the exact population and degenerate-group rule.
Replay-based task filtering is a useful hallucination check when task generation starts from a discovered executable path.
Represent experiences with both an applicability condition and content; retrieval quality depends as much on the trigger as on the advice.
A mutable live context plus immutable loss-aligned snapshots separates agent memory operations from reproducible training traces.
Report synthetic-only, target-only, and hybrid data because aggregate equivalence can hide large domain-specific reversals.
Evaluate experience both as inference-time context and as a training signal; these answer different questions about external memory versus internalization.
Use same-target sample-efficiency curves with trajectories, tokens, judge calls, time, and cost, rather than a threshold tied only to the weaker baseline.
A self-evolution claim should expose which components are autonomous and which still require profiles, proprietary teachers, reward rules, or human curation.
open_questions: Which of the two conflicting attribution encodings and normalization procedures produced the published numbers?
Do gains persist across seeds with confidence intervals and under a complete factorial ablation of all three mechanisms?
How does AgentEvolver compare at equal rollouts, tokens, judge calls, GPU-hours, and dollars with WebRL, RAGEN, GiGPO, Agent Lightning, and Tool-R1?
Can a held-out human or programmatic audit measure task validity, judge calibration, and step-attribution accuracy rather than inferring them from policy improvement?
What divergence or coverage diagnostic can detect when the generated p_train misses important regions of unknown p_target?
Does experience stripping plus selective boosting remain stable under exact off-policy correction or a critic-based estimator?
Can synthetic tasks generated in one environment improve genuinely unseen environments rather than a second API benchmark with related tool-use structure?
What is the per-rollout success distribution behind avg@8 and best@8, and how reliable is a single deployed trajectory?
How often does replay-based curation reject valid tasks or accept semantically wrong but executable tasks?
Can attribution be made counterfactual—for example by removing or replacing a step—rather than relying on retrospective LLM labels?
How robust is the self-context template when delayed dependencies exceed the compression horizon?
Do independent non-Qwen explorers and judges reproduce the gains, or are the results partly model-family self-distillation?
Can all stages be unified in one policy without catastrophic feedback loops or reward-model collapse?
What safety gate prevents open-ended task discovery from synthesizing harmful or irreversible tool operations?

competitive_landscape.title: WebRL: Training LLM Web Agents via Self-Evolving Online Curriculum Reinforcement Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: WebRL already couples automatically generated tasks, an outcome-supervised reward model, and adaptive online RL for web agents. It generates curriculum tasks from failed attempts, whereas AgentEvolver begins with profile-guided open-ended exploration and adds experience mixing plus LLM step attribution. This prior work narrows any first-self-evolving-agent or first-automatic-task-curriculum claim.

competitive_landscape.title: RAGEN: Understanding Self-Evolution in LLM Agents via Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: RAGEN/StarPO studies self-evolution, trajectory-level policy optimization, rollout freshness/diversity, reward-variance cliffs, and collapse in multi-turn agents, then stabilizes training with filtering, a critic, and gradient controls. AgentEvolver instead targets practical tool environments and adds synthetic tasks, retrieved experience, and LLM step labels, but does not run RAGEN's collapse diagnostics or equal-method comparison.

competitive_landscape.title: Group-in-Group Policy Optimization for LLM Agent Training
competitive_landscape.difference: GiGPO obtains episode- and step-level relative advantages by grouping actions from repeated anchor states, requiring no auxiliary judge or extra rollouts. AgentEvolver's self-attributing judge labels each observed step GOOD/BAD and fuses that signal with outcome reward. GiGPO is therefore a direct lower-dependency alternative that the paper cites but does not benchmark.

competitive_landscape.title: Agent Lightning: Train ANY AI Agents with Reinforcement Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: prior direct agent-RL framework and credit competitor
competitive_landscape.difference: Agent Lightning decouples arbitrary agent execution from training, defines a unified transition interface, and uses hierarchical LightningRL credit assignment across text-to-SQL, RAG, and math tool use. AgentEvolver is more prescriptive about autonomous task discovery and experience reuse and evaluates AppWorld/BFCL, but its claim to be a reusable agent-RL infrastructure should be compared with Lightning's near-zero-integration design.

competitive_landscape.title: Get Experience from Practice: LLM Agents with Record & Replay
competitive_landscape.difference: AgentRR records interaction traces, abstracts them into applicability-conditioned experiences, and replays them with explicit check functions. AgentEvolver independently uses when-to-use/content experiences, vector retrieval, and replay guidance, then additionally internalizes guided trajectories with RL and experience stripping. The experience-reuse concept is prior; the differentiator is integration into its policy-optimization loop.

competitive_landscape.title: Tool-R1: Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning for Agentic Tool Use
competitive_landscape.difference: Tool-R1 trains compositional multi-step tool use with executable Python, combines answer judgment and execution success, and reuses high-quality trajectories through a dynamic sample queue to reduce online sampling. AgentEvolver covers interactive API environments and uses natural-language experience plus dense attribution rather than cached code trajectories. Equal-sampling comparison is needed for the sample-efficiency claim.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors present AgentEvolver as a new self-evolving agent system that unifies autonomous curiosity-driven task generation, experience-guided exploration, differentiated step-level reward attribution, and a reusable training/context/environment infrastructure to make agent learning scalable, cost-effective, and continual.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The manuscript specifies the three mechanisms in Sections 3-5, integrates them in Figure 2 and the service stack in Section 6, and reports complete-system and module ablations on AppWorld and BFCL in Tables 1-7.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The broad novelty claim must be narrowed. Before AgentEvolver, WebRL already combined self-evolving task curricula and online agent RL; RAGEN studied multi-turn agent self-evolution and stability; GiGPO supplied fine-grained agent credit without an auxiliary judge; Agent Lightning decoupled general agent execution and RL training; AgentRR recorded and replayed natural-language experience; and Tool-R1 cached high-value tool trajectories for sample efficiency. What remains plausibly new is the particular integration of profile-guided path-to-task synthesis, applicability-conditioned retrieved experience that is stripped before training, positive-only clipping expansion, and whole-trajectory LLM GOOD/BAD attribution inside one AppWorld/BFCL stack. The evidence supports in-study performance and ablation gains, not first-of-kind status, proven synergy, cost-effectiveness, broad cross-domain generalization, or a fully autonomous single-model learner.

reviewer_notes: Primary full-text review of all 29 PDF pages, including equations 1-21, Tables 1-7, figures, implementation details, conclusions, and references. Official arXiv submission history was checked on 2026-08-23 and lists arXiv:2511.10395v1 as the sole/current revision; the reading is byte-pinned to the indexed local PDF and extracted text hashes above. Competitor records were checked against current official arXiv pages and exact revisions on the same date. Findings explicitly distinguish author reports, reviewer inference, and contradiction audits. Numeric 'improvements' are described as percentage points where tables contain percentages. This is not an independent secondary verification pass, and no unreported seeds, raw trajectories, source code execution, judge labels, API costs, or statistical intervals were available.
